location.value: The island of Great Britain (England, Wales and Scotland) and nearby islands, ruled from London, with a growing overseas empire.
location.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

terrain.value: An island protected by the sea, with coal and iron deposits and navigable rivers.

climate.value: Temperate maritime: mild, wet and changeable.

resources.value: Coal, iron, wool and farmland, which fuelled the early Industrial Revolution.

disasters.value: Not specifically documented in the sources checked.

population.value: Not in the Wikipedia infobox. Great Britain grew from about 7 million (1707) to about 10.5 million by the 1801 census.

urbanisation.value: London was Europe’s largest city. Industrial towns such as Manchester and Birmingham grew from the late 18th century.

disease.value: Smallpox was common. Jenner’s cowpox vaccine (1796) began its decline.

migration.value: Settlers to North America and the Caribbean, and transported convicts (to Australia from 1788).
migration.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

economicBase.value: Agriculture, commerce and finance, and from about 1760 the Industrial Revolution (textiles, steam power). Mercantilism governed colonial trade.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

tradeRoutes.value: Atlantic trade, including sugar and the slave trade. The East India Company gained control of Bengal after Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764).
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

wealth.value: One of the richest countries in Europe per person by the late 18th century.

moneyAndTax.value: The pound sterling, the Bank of England and a strong national debt system (the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720 notwithstanding).
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

inequality.value: Highly hierarchical: a small landed elite controlled Parliament and the land.
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

governmentType.value: A unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy with a single Parliament at Westminster.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox)

keyRulers.value: Queen Anne (1707–1714), George I, George II, George III (1760–1820). Prime ministers Robert Walpole (1721–1742, the first) and William Pitt the Younger (1783–1801).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox)

succession.value: A Protestant succession under the Act of Settlement (1701), which brought the Hanoverian dynasty in 1714.
succession.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

institutions.value: The Acts of Union (1707) united England and Scotland, keeping Scots law and the Church of Scotland. The cabinet system and prime minister developed under Walpole.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox)

stability.value: Jacobite risings (1715, 1745), defeated at Culloden (1746). The Irish Rebellion of 1798 led to the union with Ireland.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the Whig and Tory parties. Walpole’s patronage system was criticised as corrupt.
eliteConflict.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

armyAndTech.value: The Royal Navy became the world’s strongest.

majorWars.value: The War of the Spanish Succession (to 1714). The Seven Years’ War (1756–63). The American Revolutionary War (1775–83). The French Revolutionary Wars (from 1793).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Gained Gibraltar, Newfoundland and Acadia (1713) and New France (1763), but lost the Thirteen Colonies (1783). Settled New South Wales (from 1788).
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

alliancesRivals.value: The main rival was France. Also Spain, and the American revolutionaries. Allies were Prussia, Portugal and Hanover.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

inventions.value: The Industrial Revolution: the spinning jenny, the water frame, and Watt’s improved steam engine (1776).

scienceEducation.value: The Scottish Enlightenment (Hume, Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations, 1776) and the Royal Society.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

openness.value: Open to trade and new ideas, with a relatively free press.

communicationTransport.value: Turnpike roads, stagecoaches and canals (Bridgewater Canal, 1761); a merchant navy; the Royal Mail.

religion.value: Anglican (Church of England) and Presbyterian (Church of Scotland). Catholics and Dissenters faced legal restrictions. The Evangelical revival (Wesley).
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox)

languageWriting.value: English, plus Scots, Welsh and Scottish Gaelic.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox)

artsArchitecture.value: Georgian architecture, Augustan literature (Pope, Swift), Johnson’s Dictionary (1755) and Handel’s music.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

socialStructure.value: Aristocracy and gentry, merchants, an emerging industrial middle class, labourers. Slavery was legal in the colonies.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: A new “British” identity built on Protestantism, the monarchy and rivalry with France.

dailyLife.value: Brick and stone cottages and town houses; bread, beer, cheese, tea becoming popular; long working days in early factories.

neighbours.value: France, Ireland (separate kingdom in personal union), the Dutch Republic, Spain and Portugal.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

ideasReligions.value: Exported Enlightenment political ideas (Locke, Smith), Protestant missions, and parliamentary practice.

colonisation.value: The “First British Empire” in North America and the Caribbean (including slave plantations), and the East India Company’s conquests in India.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

riseSignals.value: The union of England and Scotland (1707), naval supremacy, financial institutions, colonial trade, and the Industrial Revolution.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: After victory in the Seven Years’ War (1763), the dominant colonial power.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: Not a decline: the loss of the American colonies (1783) shifted focus to Asia, the Pacific and Africa.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

outcome.value: Transformation. Under the Acts of Union 1800, it merged with Ireland on 1 January 1801 to form the United Kingdom, which led the British Empire.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Parliamentary and state records, the 1801 census, and contemporary writing. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (mostly the infobox). See also Colley (1992).
sources.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: High for events. Population before the 1801 census is estimated. The end is dated 31 December 1800 or 1 January 1801.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Britain (checked 5 Nov 2026)
